text.p: The following is a direct contribution from commodity statistician F.O. Licht in Ratzeburg, Germany. Please address any queries to Helmut Ahlfeld on +00 49 4541 88920.

Robusta futures in London closed below the highs but above Friday's close. May closed $1 higher at $1,641 per tonne, while July added $8 to close at $1,670 per tonne. The Colombian truck drivers' strike had little influence in London. It is generally believed that the new strike is likely to be less disruptive than the crippling stoppage in October.

Arabica futures in New York ended mostly lower with front month May losing 1.65 cents/lb to close at 214.90 cents/lb, while July gave up 10 points to close at 194.05 cents/lb. News that Colombia's truck drivers had gone ahead with a long-planned work stoppage briefly drove prices up to new life-of-contract highs. However, news that Brazil's port workers had ended their work stoppage after two days, coupled with nervousness ahead of May's first notice day on Tuesday, quickly put an end to the rally.

Today's weaker tone does not mean the end of the market's bullish tone, as supplies must be expected to remain tight. Some analysts are firmly convinced, that the peak has not yet been reached and that further price rises are a definite possibility. After the close of trading, the CSCE reported a further fall of certified coffee stocks, which underlines current tight supplies.
UNITED STATES - US certified coffee stocks fell by 2,250 bags on April 18 to 61,099 bags. There were 500 bags pending grading in New York.

COLOMBIA - According to trade sources the strike by Colombia's main truck drivers' union will affect deliveries against May contracts if it lasts more than ten days. The strike by the Colombian Truck Drivers' Association (ACC) which represents about 80 per cent of Colombia's truckers, was called in March on grounds that the government, and private transportation companies, failed to fulfill terms of an accord that ended a crippling, 11-days strike in October.
The latest strike comes as Colombia's coffee growers are just beginning to harvest the so-called 'mitaca' crop, which accounts for about 40 per cent of yearly production.

BRAZIL - Brazil trade house Tristao has raised its production estimate for 1996/97 to 27.5 mn bags, up from its previous forecast of 25.85 mn bags. Production in 1997/98 is estimated at 23.5 mn bags. The company said that the drop in output is partly cyclical in nature.

NETHERLANDS - The Netherlands imported 252,956 bags of coffee in November 1996, 2 per cent less than was imported the same month the previous year. That brought total imports since the beginning of 1996 up to 2.909 mn bags, 8.5 per cent more than was imported the same period in 1995. Total imports in calendar year 1995 dropped by 1.8 per cent to 2.910 mn bags.

Main suppliers of green coffee in January/November 1996 were Uganda (167,000 vs 199,000 bags), El Salvador (198,900 vs 89,000 bags), Brazil (144,100 vs 343,100 bags) and Colombia (414,800 vs 393,000 bags). The country exported 529,100 bags of coffee in January/November 1996, nearly 6 per cent less than was exported the same period in 1995. Total exports in calendar year 1995 dropped by 15 per cent to 616,900 bags.
